# PERPETUAL → SUBSCRIPTION: BUSINESS-MODEL TRANSITION PLAN
**Board decision document · v1.0 · For approval at Gate 0**

> **Numbers discipline.** Every figure in this document is a **design target or illustrative model output built on a stated assumption set**, not a measured result. The baseline is scaled to an illustrative $500M-revenue company; §7 lists the assumptions and flags the three that actually move the answer. Before external use, Finance and IR must re-run §6 on audited actuals and re-verify the competitor precedents in §5.4.

---

## The decision in one paragraph

We move to subscription over **five years, not one quarter**, using a **three-lane offer** — legacy perpetual stays alive and honored forever, a **term-license bridge lane** for customers who cannot or will not go cloud, and full subscription as the default and the only lane that receives new capability. We never revoke anything: the competitor that lost a fifth of its installed base did not lose it to subscriptions, it lost it to **forced migration plus a simultaneous price shock**, and we design the exact inverse — a "no worse off in year 1" price guarantee, a loyalty credit for historical maintenance spend, and a published maintenance-sunset calendar customers can plan against. We price subscription at **~38% of perpetual list per seat-year**, which is accretive to a maintained customer's lifetime value from year 3 but dilutive to recognized revenue in years 1–3; the resulting trough is a **~25% peak-to-trough revenue decline bottoming in FY3, with ARR crossing above FY0 revenue in FY5 and free cash flow troughing a year earlier and half as deep as EPS**. Sales keeps its earnings through a **24-month OTE bridge plus a 2.5× quota-credit multiple on multi-year subscription ACV**, which is the single highest-attrition risk in the plan and is funded explicitly rather than hoped for. Investors are moved to a new scoreboard — ARR, cRPO, NRR, billings, FCF — **two quarters before the trough begins, with the trough map published in advance**, quarterly EPS guidance withdrawn, and executive incentive comp re-cut off EPS onto ARR/NRR/FCF so we are not asking the board to tolerate an EPS decline while paying management to prevent one.

---

## 1. What we are deliberately NOT doing

These are exclusions, not oversights. Each one is a lever we are consciously leaving in the drawer.

| Excluded | Why |
|---|---|
| **Forced migration / any conversion deadline that ends a working license** | This is the specific mechanism that cost the competitor ~20% of its base. There is no version of this plan that includes a kill switch, a phone-home expiry, or "your perpetual license stops working." |
| **Cloud-only** | Regulated, air-gapped, and infrastructure-constrained customers are a meaningful minority of enterprise seats. Forcing them to cloud converts a pricing conversation into a displacement RFP. The term-license lane exists for them. |
| **Big-bang single-quarter cutover** | Removes all optionality and all learning. We stage by segment, with kill/adjust gates. |
| **Simultaneous product re-platforming** | We are changing the *commercial* model. Changing the architecture at the same time means every commercial failure is blamed on a bug and vice versa. Re-platform work continues on its own roadmap and is not a transition dependency. |
| **Usage/consumption pricing in v1** | Attractive long-term; unforecastable during a trough. Revisit at Gate 4. |
| **Moving professional services to subscription** | Services stay project-priced. Bundling them hides the ARR signal. |
| **Raising list price in the same 12 months as the migration offer** | Price increase and model change must never arrive in the same envelope. |
| **Discounting below the floor in §3.3 to hit a conversion number** | The floor is a permanent price reset if breached. Conversion pace is negotiable; the floor is not. |

---

## 2. Offer structure and migration incentives

### 2.1 The entitlement question, answered

The blocking emotional issue is not price. It is that a customer who paid $250,000 for a perpetual license in 2016 believes they bought something permanent and is being told it was a rental. **They are right, and we should say so in writing.** The following is drafted to be published verbatim, signed by the CEO, and repeated identically by every rep:

> **The Perpetual Promise**
>
> 1. **Your perpetual license is perpetual.** The version you own will run, forever, with no expiry, no phone-home check, and no remote deactivation. We will never ship a change that disables a license you paid for.
> 2. **We will keep it running.** Security patches and critical defect fixes for your current major version through **[Date, ≥36 months from announcement]**. Certification against new OS and database releases through **[Date, ≥24 months]**.
> 3. **What changes, and when you'll know.** New features ship only in the subscription and term lanes. Maintenance remains purchasable, at a published, pre-announced escalation schedule (§2.3), until **[Sunset Date, 48 months from announcement]**.
> 4. **If you move, we credit what you've already paid.** See the loyalty credit (§2.4). Your first subscription year will not cost more than your current maintenance year.
> 5. **If you never move, that is a legitimate choice.** You remain a customer in good standing. We will not stop taking your call.

Point 5 matters as much as point 1. Internally we model non-movers as a **declining annuity**, not as a failure. A customer who pays maintenance for six more years and then leaves is worth more than a customer we churned in year 1 by pushing.

### 2.2 Three lanes

| | **Lane A — Legacy Perpetual + Maintenance** | **Lane B — Term License (bridge)** | **Lane C — Subscription (default)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Who** | Non-movers, capex-locked buyers, long-tail | On-prem-required: regulated, air-gapped, data-residency, latency-bound | Everyone else; all new business after Gate 3 |
| **Rights** | Owned version, forever. Maintenance = patches + certs only | Time-boxed license, on-prem, full updates, 1/3/5-yr terms | Hosted or on-prem, full updates, all new capability, cloud services |
| **New features** | **No** — frozen at last major version at sunset | Yes | Yes, first |
| **Status** | Open but frozen; closed to *new* license sales at Gate 4 | Open indefinitely | Growing to ~100% of new business |
| **Rev rec** | License point-in-time (historic); maintenance ratable | **License element point-in-time; support/updates ratable** (§6.3) | Fully ratable |
| **Strategic role** | Don't churn them | **The trough dial** | The destination |

**Lane B is the most important design choice in this document and the one most transitions omit.** It does three things at once: it removes "you're forcing us to the cloud" from every enterprise negotiation; it preserves a point-in-time revenue element under ASC 606, which is a *deliberate, tunable lever on trough depth*; and it gives the sales force a deal shape that still feels large. Its cost is that it partially reintroduces lumpiness at renewal and that investors assign term-license ARR a lower quality multiple than SaaS ARR. We therefore **cap Lane B at ~30% of subscription bookings mix** and hold the cap as a stated policy (§6.3 shows the sensitivity).

### 2.3 Maintenance sunset calendar — published on day one

Predictability is the anti-churn mechanism. Customers forgive escalation they saw coming three years out; they do not forgive a surprise.

| Date (from announcement) | Event |
|---|---|
| **T+0** | Announcement. Perpetual Promise published. Migration offer opens. Maintenance renewal price **held flat** for 12 months. |
| **T+12 mo** | Maintenance uplift **+8%**; no new perpetual features shipped from this date. |
| **T+24 mo** | Maintenance uplift **+12%**. New perpetual license sales restricted to existing-account expansion only. |
| **T+30 mo (Gate 4)** | **Perpetual list withdrawn** for new logos. |
| **T+36 mo** | Maintenance uplift **+15%**. Final security-patch commitment window begins. |
| **T+48 mo** | **Maintenance sunset.** Lane A becomes self-supported. Loyalty credit expires. |

Cumulative maintenance escalation ≈ +38% over four years. That is deliberate: it must be large enough to make the subscription lane obviously cheaper by T+24, and gradual enough that no single renewal conversation contains a shock. **Any enterprise account may negotiate a bespoke sunset extension of up to 24 months** — that is a retention tool, priced, and approved by the deal desk, not a leak.

### 2.4 Migration incentives

| Incentive | Design | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **"No worse off in year 1" guarantee** | Year-1 subscription invoice ≤ customer's current annual maintenance invoice. Uplift arrives via a published step: Y1 = maintenance parity, Y2 = +15%, Y3 = +15%, then locked. | Removes the price-shock mechanism that broke the competitor. Costs us ~2 years of uplift; buys us the base. |
| **Loyalty

# SNACK LINE FOR JAPAN — TEN CONCEPTS ACROSS SEVEN CONSUMPTION OCCASIONS
**Product Council decision document | v2.0**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Market: Japan.** Chosen because it rewards format and texture novelty faster than any comparable market, has a dense, high-turnover convenience and gifting infrastructure that lets a small line reach scale without national listings, and has a well-documented occasion grammar we can design against rather than guess at. (Selection scoring is in Appendix A; if the Council has already fixed a different market, swap the market and the concepts below hold their *structure* but not their flavor logic — treat §2 as re-buildable in four weeks.)

**Portfolio thesis:** we are not launching one snack in ten flavors. We are launching **five distinct manufacturing platforms** — roasted legume, thin baked rice-and-seaweed sheet, baked mochi, freeze-dried fruit with coating, and extruded/puffed protein — deployed as **ten SKUs across seven occasions**, so that a failure in any one occasion does not orphan a plant investment. The portfolio is weighted to three occasions we believe are simultaneously large, under-served by imported product, and reachable without a national retail negotiation: **with-alcohol (*otsumami*), gifting/souvenir (*omiyage*), and late-night study-or-overtime fuel.** Everything else in the ten is coverage or seasonal ammunition.

**One design constraint governs all ten:** the Two-Anchor Rule (§4) — each SKU carries at most one thing the shopper has to be *taught*.

---

## 1. The seven occasions we are designing against

These are not dayparts. They are purchase rituals with different shoppers, price tolerances, pack behaviors, and channels.

| # | Occasion | Who / when | What the pack must do | Price tolerance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **O1** | **Omiyage / gifting** — station kiosk, dept. store basement, airport | Traveler buying *for others*; obligation purchase | Individually wrapped units, divisible for an office, regional or seasonal story, box that survives a train | High (¥1,000–2,000/box) |
| **O2** | **Konbini solo desk lunch add-on** | Office worker, 11:30–13:30, buying with an onigiri/bento | Read in 2 seconds on a crowded shelf; not messy at a desk; one-hand eating | Low (¥150–260) |
| **O3** | **Otsumami — with alcohol** | 20:00–23:00, home drinking, beer/highball/sake; skews M25–55 | Salt and umami depth, slow-eat texture, resealable, sits next to the can | Mid (¥250–400) |
| **O4** | **Oyatsu / tea-time (15:00)** | Adults, often female, with sencha or coffee; also *at-home guest* use | Restrained sweetness, aroma-forward, visually neat on a small plate | Mid–high (¥300–600) |
| **O5** | **Kids after-school & bento add-in** | Purchased by a parent, eaten by a 4–10 y/o | Portion-controlled, low sodium, no allergen surprises, parent-legible nutrition | Low (¥120–200) |
| **O6** | **Late-night study / overtime fuel** | 18–29 students & juniors, 22:00–02:00; also gaming | Resealable, non-greasy fingers (keyboard-safe), function claim (protein, caffeine-free) | Mid (¥250–350) |
| **O7** | **Seasonal / festival limited edition** | Everyone; hanami, summer, autumn, New Year | Time-bound reason to buy; drives trial of the base platform | Follows host occasion |

**Deliberate gaps.** We are *not* entering: breakfast (owned by bread and yogurt), chilled dessert cabinet (cold-chain we don't have), gum/mints (dominated, no platform fit), and character-licensed kids' confection (license economics kill margin at our volume). These are exclusions, not oversights.

---

## 2. The ten concepts

**Reading note.** Every sweetness, salt, and shelf-life figure below is a **design target for bench work, not a measured value.** Benchmark measurement against named retail comparators is a Gate 1 deliverable (§5). Texture targets are given in Japanese texture vocabulary because that is the language the category's package copy and consumer panels actually use — *sakusaku* (light dry shatter), *kari-kari* (hard dry crunch), *mochi-mochi* (elastic chew), *shittori* (moist-dense), *fuwafuwa* (airy melt).

---

### C1 — SHIO-KŌJI KARI-KARI
*Roasted legume platform · flagship otsumami*

- **Occasion:** O3 primary · O6 secondary
- **Flavor logic:** Depth without heat. *Shio-kōji* (salt-fermented rice culture) gives glutamate-driven savoriness, so we hit umami saturation at roughly **0.8× the sodium** of a mainstream fried broad-bean otsumami. The pitch to the shopper is "salty enough, less salt" — a claim that works on both the drinker and the person in the household who buys for him.
- **Key ingredients:** Broad bean (*soramame*), roasted edamame, shio-kōji seasoning, kombu extract, sesame oil trace, black pepper.
- **Texture target:** *kari-kari* — hard, slow, deliberately effortful. Bite force is the product; this is the anti-crisp.
- **Format & pack:** 55 g resealable stand pouch, matte black, ~6 min eating duration to match one can.
- **Channel & price:** Convenience liquor bay, supermarket alcohol aisle, drug store. **¥298.**
- **Supply route:** Export from existing nut/legume roasting line; seasoning applied post-roast, so no new equipment.
- **Shelf life / climate:** 12 mo ambient. Aw ≤0.35 with oxygen absorber; legumes go rancid-then-soft in a Japanese August, so lipid oxidation and pouch OTR are the spec risks, not microbiology.
- **Certification gate:** Additive positive-list check on the kōji seasoning carrier; soy and sesame allergen declaration.
- **Biggest risk:** *Kari-kari* hardness is a real barrier for shoppers over 60. Mitigation: this SKU is not aimed at them; do not soften it to widen it.

---

### C2 — UMI-NO-HA CRISPS
*Thin baked rice-and-seaweed sheet platform · konbini workhorse*

- **Occasion:** O2 primary · O3 secondary
- **Flavor logic:** Nori is the single most familiar savory flavor in the market, which buys us permission for the novelty vector: **yuzu-wasabi** aroma applied as a cold-dusted top note so it hits the nose before the tongue. Sodium target parity with a standard soy rice cracker; heat kept low (*wasabi* as fragrance, not burn).
- **Key ingredients:** Japanese short-grain rice flour, pressed *nori*, yuzu peel powder, wasabi flavor, light soy, rice bran oil.
- **Texture target:** *sakusaku* — 0.6 mm sheet that shatters silently. Must not shed crumbs onto a keyboard or a bento lid.
- **Format & pack:** 8 sheets in 4 twin-wrapped pairs, 30 g flat sleeve that fits an inside jacket pocket.
- **Channel & price:** Convenience store, station kiosk. **¥178.**
- **Supply route:** **Local co-pack.** Rice-cracker baking is not a capability we should build; domestic *senbei* co-packers exist at our volume and eliminate the freight-crush problem for a fragile sheet.
- **Shelf life / climate:** 8 mo. Nori is hygroscopic — it goes leathery long before it goes unsafe. Twin-wrap is a shelf-life decision, not a portioning one.
- **Certification gate:** Domestic-origin labeling for rice; standard Food Labeling Act pack layout.
- **Biggest risk:** The shelf is crowded and margins are thin at ¥178. If it cannot win on aroma at first bite, it has nothing.

---

### C3 — MOCHI-MOCHI KUBE
*Baked mochi platform · tea-time centerpiece*

- **Occasion:** O4 primary · O1 secondary
- **Flavor logic:** *Kinako* (roasted soy flour) and black-sesame with a *kurozatō* (black sugar) glaze — three flavors that need no explanation. Sugar target **~0.65× a mainstream milk-chocolate biscuit**, because the occasion's shopper is actively avoiding sweetness, not seeking it.
- **Key ingredients:** Glutinous rice, kinako, black sesame paste, Okinawan black sugar, sea salt.
- **Texture target:** Dual-phase — a *sakusaku* baked shell yielding to a *mochi-mochi* interior. **This is the portfolio's signature technical claim** and the hardest thing in the ten to manufacture.
- **Format & pack:** 12 × 8 g cubes, individually wrapped, in a rigid 96 g tray-box.
- **Channel & price:** Supermarket confection, department-store food hall. **¥398.**
- **Supply route:** Local co-pack, mandatory — baked-mochi expertise does not exist in our plants, and the two-phase texture will not survive 30 days of ocean freight.
- **Shelf life / climate:** 90 days, the shortest in the portfolio. Moisture migration from core to shell is the whole engineering problem; retrogradation of the starch is the clock.
- **Certification gate:** Soy allergen; sesame recommended-allergen declaration.
- **Biggest risk:** Highest technical risk in the ten. **Recommend an explicit kill-or-continue decision at Gate 2** rather than letting it absorb development budget by momentum.

---

### C4 — KAORI-BIN (Aroma Flight)
*Assortment of C1/C2/C3 platforms · gifting engine*

- **Occasion:** O1 primary · O7 secondary
- **Flavor logic:** Not a new recipe — a new *reason*. Four regional aroma stories (Shizuoka green tea, Setouchi lemon, Hokkaidō kombu-butter, Kyūshū smoked soy), three units each, in a flight the buyer can hand around an office. The gifting shopper is buying a story and a division count, not a taste.
- **Key ingredients:** Draws on C1–C3 bases with four seasoning packages; single named regional ingredient per compartment as the proof point.
- **Texture target:** Deliberately varied across compartments — variety is the product.
- **Format & pack:** 12 individually wrapped units, 4 compartments, rigid box with *noshi*-compatible sleeve, ~180 g.
- **Channel & price:** Station kiosk, airport, department-store basement, corporate gifting. **¥1,480.**
- **Supply route:** Domestic assembly and boxing next to the co-packers; boxing offshore is not viable at gifting cosmetic standards.
- **Shelf life / climate:** Constrained to the *shortest* member — so **C3 is excluded from v1 of the box** unless Gate 2 delivers 120 days. Ship v1 with C1, C2 and a fourth stable base.
- **Certification gate:** Consolidated allergen matrix for the whole box; regional-origin claims must be substantiated per compartment.
- **Biggest risk:** Gifting shelf space is relationship-gated and seasonally allocated. Without a distributor who already places *omiyage*, this SKU has no route. **This is the portfolio's single biggest commercial dependency.**

---

### C5 — DASHI-MARU
*Puffed grain platform · konbini second shot*

- **Occasion:** O2 primary · O5 secondary
- **Flavor logic:** *Katsuo* (bonito) dashi and toasted sesame on a puffed sorghum-and-brown-rice ball. Familiar flavor in an unfamiliar geometry — spherical, so it works one-handed and doesn't stack in a pocket. Sodium at **0.85× a standard cheese puff**, with dashi carrying the gap.
- **Key ingredients:** Sorghum, brown rice, bonito extract, kombu, sesame, soy.
- **Texture target:** *fuwafuwa*-to-*sakusaku* — collapses fast, low chew load, deliberately the inverse of C1.
- **Format & pack:** 40 g pillow pouch, single-serve, non-resealable (a deliberate "finish it now" pack).
- **Channel & price:** Convenience store, vending, campus stores. **¥168.**
- **Supply route:** Export from existing extrusion capacity — this is the lowest-cost SKU to launch and should be the volume floor of the portfolio.
- **Shelf life / climate:** 10 mo. Puffed product bruises in freight; case-crush spec matters more than the recipe.
- **Certification gate:** Fish (bonito) allergen declaration; check bonito extract carrier against the additive positive list.
- **Biggest risk:** Least differentiated concept in the set. Justified as capacity utilization and price-point coverage, **not** as a hero.

---

### C6 — YUZU KŌRI
*Freeze-dried fruit + coating platform · premium tea-time and gift filler*

- **Occasion:** O4 primary · O1 secondary
- **Flavor logic:** Freeze-dried mikan segments and candied yuzu peel, half-dipped in white chocolate. Acid does the work sugar usually does; total sugar target **~0.6×** a comparable coated-fruit confection. The visible undipped half is the honesty signal — the shopper can see real fruit.
- **Key ingredients:** Mikan, yuzu peel, white chocolate (cocoa butter, not substitute fat), trace sea salt.
- **Texture target:** *shuwa*-crisp melt — dry-crisp fruit collapsing to juice on the tongue, then the fat coating. Absolutely no chew.
- **Format & pack:** 45 g resealable window pouch; the window is doing the

- Assumptions must be labeled as assumptions, with the two or three that actually move the answer flagged.

### 4. Format expectations for the retry

One-paragraph decision summary; explicit "what we are deliberately not doing"; a phased timeline with named gates and kill/adjust criteria; a quantified trough table; a risk register with owners; and a stated position on the entitlement question that a long-standing customer could read without feeling robbed. Avoid inventing precise figures without labeling them as targets.

# PERPETUAL → SUBSCRIPTION: BUSINESS-MODEL TRANSITION PLAN
**Board decision document · v1.0 · For approval at Gate 0**

> **Numbers discipline.** Every figure in this document is a **design target or illustrative model output built on a stated assumption set**, not a measured result. The baseline is scaled to an illustrative $500M-revenue company; §7 lists the assumptions and flags the three that actually move the answer. Before external use, Finance and IR must re-run §6 on audited actuals and re-verify the competitor precedents in §5.4.

---

## The decision in one paragraph

We move to subscription over **five years, not one quarter**, using a **three-lane offer** — legacy perpetual stays alive and honored forever, a **term-license bridge lane** for customers who cannot or will not go cloud, and full subscription as the default and the only lane that receives new capability. We never revoke anything: the competitor that lost a fifth of its installed base did not lose it to subscriptions, it lost it to **forced migration plus a simultaneous price shock**, and we design the exact inverse — a "no worse off in year 1" price guarantee, a loyalty credit for historical maintenance spend, and a published maintenance-sunset calendar customers can plan against. We price subscription at **~38% of perpetual list per seat-year**, which is accretive to a maintained customer's lifetime value from year 3 but dilutive to recognized revenue in years 1–3; the resulting trough is a **~25% peak-to-trough revenue decline bottoming in FY3, with ARR crossing above FY0 revenue in FY5 and free cash flow troughing a year earlier and half as deep as EPS**. Sales keeps its earnings through a **24-month OTE bridge plus a 2.5× quota-credit multiple on multi-year subscription ACV**, which is the single highest-attrition risk in the plan and is funded explicitly rather than hoped for. Investors are moved to a new scoreboard — ARR, cRPO, NRR, billings, FCF — **two quarters before the trough begins, with the trough map published in advance**, quarterly EPS guidance withdrawn, and executive incentive comp re-cut off EPS onto ARR/NRR/FCF so we are not asking the board to tolerate an EPS decline while paying management to prevent one.

---

## 1. What we are deliberately NOT doing

These are exclusions, not oversights. Each one is a lever we are consciously leaving in the drawer.

| Excluded | Why |
|---|---|
| **Forced migration / any conversion deadline that ends a working license** | This is the specific mechanism that cost the competitor ~20% of its base. There is no version of this plan that includes a kill switch, a phone-home expiry, or "your perpetual license stops working." |
| **Cloud-only** | Regulated, air-gapped, and infrastructure-constrained customers are a meaningful minority of enterprise seats. Forcing them to cloud converts a pricing conversation into a displacement RFP. The term-license lane exists for them. |
| **Big-bang single-quarter cutover** | Removes all optionality and all learning. We stage by segment, with kill/adjust gates. |
| **Simultaneous product re-platforming** | We are changing the *commercial* model. Changing the architecture at the same time means every commercial failure is blamed on a bug and vice versa. Re-platform work continues on its own roadmap and is not a transition dependency. |
| **Usage/consumption pricing in v1** | Attractive long-term; unforecastable during a trough. Revisit at Gate 4. |
| **Moving professional services to subscription** | Services stay project-priced. Bundling them hides the ARR signal. |
| **Raising list price in the same 12 months as the migration offer** | Price increase and model change must never arrive in the same envelope. |
| **Discounting below the floor in §3.3 to hit a conversion number** | The floor is a permanent price reset if breached. Conversion pace is negotiable; the floor is not. |

---

## 2. Offer structure and migration incentives

### 2.1 The entitlement question, answered

The blocking emotional issue is not price. It is that a customer who paid $250,000 for a perpetual license in 2016 believes they bought something permanent and is being told it was a rental. **They are right, and we should say so in writing.** The following is drafted to be published verbatim, signed by the CEO, and repeated identically by every rep:

> **The Perpetual Promise**
>
> 1. **Your perpetual license is perpetual.** The version you own will run, forever, with no expiry, no phone-home check, and no remote deactivation. We will never ship a change that disables a license you paid for.
> 2. **We will keep it running.** Security patches and critical defect fixes for your current major version through **[Date, ≥36 months from announcement]**. Certification against new OS and database releases through **[Date, ≥24 months]**.
> 3. **What changes, and when you'll know.** New features ship only in the subscription and term lanes. Maintenance remains purchasable, at a published, pre-announced escalation schedule (§2.3), until **[Sunset Date, 48 months from announcement]**.
> 4. **If you move, we credit what you've already paid.** See the loyalty credit (§2.4). Your first subscription year will not cost more than your current maintenance year.
> 5. **If you never move, that is a legitimate choice.** You remain a customer in good standing. We will not stop taking your call.

Point 5 matters as much as point 1. Internally we model non-movers as a **declining annuity**, not as a failure. A customer who pays maintenance for six more years and then leaves is worth more than a customer we churned in year 1 by pushing.

### 2.2 Three lanes

| | **Lane A — Legacy Perpetual + Maintenance** | **Lane B — Term License (bridge)** | **Lane C — Subscription (default)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Who** | Non-movers, capex-locked buyers, long-tail | On-prem-required: regulated, air-gapped, data-residency, latency-bound | Everyone else; all new business after Gate 3 |
| **Rights** | Owned version, forever. Maintenance = patches + certs only | Time-boxed license, on-prem, full updates, 1/3/5-yr terms | Hosted or on-prem, full updates, all new capability, cloud services |
| **New features** | **No** — frozen at last major version at sunset | Yes | Yes, first |
| **Status** | Open but frozen; closed to *new* license sales at Gate 4 | Open indefinitely | Growing to ~100% of new business |
| **Rev rec** | License point-in-time (historic); maintenance ratable | **License element point-in-time; support/updates ratable** (§6.3) | Fully ratable |
| **Strategic role** | Don't churn them | **The trough dial** | The destination |

**Lane B is the most important design choice in this document and the one most transitions omit.** It does three things at once: it removes "you're forcing us to the cloud" from every enterprise negotiation; it preserves a point-in-time revenue element under ASC 606, which is a *deliberate, tunable lever on trough depth*; and it gives the sales force a deal shape that still feels large. Its cost is that it partially reintroduces lumpiness at renewal and that investors assign term-license ARR a lower quality multiple than SaaS ARR. We therefore **cap Lane B at ~30% of subscription bookings mix** and hold the cap as a stated policy (§6.3 shows the sensitivity).

### 2.3 Maintenance sunset calendar — published on day one

Predictability is the anti-churn mechanism. Customers forgive escalation they saw coming three years out; they do not forgive a surprise.

| Date (from announcement) | Event |
|---|---|
| **T+0** | Announcement. Perpetual Promise published. Migration offer opens. Maintenance renewal price **held flat** for 12 months. |
| **T+12 mo** | Maintenance uplift **+8%**; no new perpetual features shipped from this date. |
| **T+24 mo** | Maintenance uplift **+12%**. New perpetual license sales restricted to existing-account expansion only. |
| **T+30 mo (Gate 4)** | **Perpetual list withdrawn** for new logos. |
| **T+36 mo** | Maintenance uplift **+15%**. Final security-patch commitment window begins. |
| **T+48 mo** | **Maintenance sunset.** Lane A becomes self-supported. Loyalty credit expires. |

Cumulative maintenance escalation ≈ +38% over four years. That is deliberate: it must be large enough to make the subscription lane obviously cheaper by T+24, and gradual enough that no single renewal conversation contains a shock. **Any enterprise account may negotiate a bespoke sunset extension of up to 24 months** — that is a retention tool, priced, and approved by the deal desk, not a leak.

| **"No worse off in year 1" guarantee** | Year-1 subscription invoice ≤ customer's current annual maintenance invoice.
